content: HIV testing is provided to clients in the privacy of their homes, adhering strictly to Pakistan's national guidelines. Pre-test counseling includes detailed information about the risks of acquiring HIV, an explanation of the testing process, and an assessment of the client’s ability to cope with a potential positive result. If the test result is negative, clients are advised to seek follow-up testing in three months. For those who test positive, post-test counseling is conducted to establish referrals for ongoing care and support, including antiretroviral therapy (ART) and family planning services. All client records are maintained with strict confidentiality protocols using the Nai Zindagi client information management system. Condom distribution is an integral part of service delivery for all clients, and nutritional support packages are provided every three months. Among 54,192 people who inject drugs registered under the program, 19,079 (35%) had reactive HIV test results, and of these, 5,660 (30%) were married. To date, 4,131 (72%) of the spouses and partners of HIV-positive individuals who inject drugs have been tested in 24,598 HIV testing episodes, with 365 (8%) testing reactive. Of these, 280 (81%) have been successfully linked to ART. The program has demonstrated the feasibility of delivering community-based harm reduction and HIV testing services to spouses and partners of people who inject drugs in Pakistan. Population Services International leads the USAID-funded Going the Last Mile for HIV Control program in Zimbabwe, supporting the Ministry of Health and Child Care’s efforts to achieve HIV epidemic control. This program focuses on identifying new HIV-positive clients, linking them to treatment, and retaining them in care, with a specific emphasis on hard-to-reach populations, including men who have sex with men and female sex workers. Enhanced peer mobilizers (EPMs) are recruited, trained, and equipped to engage their peer networks with key messages about HIV/AIDS and to incentivize linking their peers to clinical services. Clients who test HIV-positive are encouraged to bring a peer for testing and to share contacts within their sexual and social networks, which are then followed up with HIV testing services through index case testing. Nurse testers provide community-based index testing for these contacts. Data from the New Africa House testing site in Harare during the first quarter of the US Government fiscal year 2019 showed that 92% of 219 HIV-positive key populations were offered index testing. A 5:1 index-to-contact ratio was achieved, with 81% of contacts tested for HIV, and 37% of those testing positive. Among those who tested positive, 97% were referred for ART, and 94% of those referred were successfully linked to ART. The Assisted Partner Services (aPS) Scale-up Study, funded by the NIH and implemented by the University of Washington and PATH, evaluates the integration of aPS into real-world settings. This study builds on a cluster-randomized trial in Kenya, which demonstrated that tracing and testing the sexual partners of HIV-infected adults was safe and significantly increased the identification of HIV-positive men in need of care and treatment. The study is being conducted at 31 government health facilities and nine DREAMS spaces in two high-HIV-burden counties in Kenya, enrolling index female clients and their male sexual contacts. Index clients are counseled on partner notification, and their male partners are anonymously notified of potential HIV exposure and offered testing. Newly identified clients are immediately linked to care and started on ART, with follow-up at six weeks, six months, and 12 months to assess care linkage, ART initiation, and viral suppression. Serodiscordant partners are referred for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV transmission. From May 2018 to February 2019, 555 HIV-positive index female clients were identified, providing details of 694 male sexual contacts. Of these, 361 male contacts were traced and offered HIV testing, with 188 identified as HIV-positive (52% positivity rate). Among these, 74 were newly identified as HIV-positive, representing 21% of all male contacts traced and tested. All HIV-positive individuals were immediately linked to care and treatment. This approach has proven effective in identifying HIV-positive males and ensuring their enrollment in care and treatment. Online platforms have emerged as powerful tools for reaching hard-to-reach populations. In Vietnam, most men who have sex with men and transgender women use social media to seek sexual partners and information about HIV. Online outreach efforts involve interconnected communication channels, including dedicated Facebook pages, online peer influencers, gay hookup apps, an HIV service booking app (I Reserve), and AI/chatbots. These platforms provide a dynamic entry point for HIV self-testing, ART, and PrEP services. Online peer influencers (OPIs) are trained to provide counseling on sexual health issues, refer at-risk individuals for HIV services, facilitate online HIV self-test orders, and conduct offline community-based testing. An online survey of 3,989 users of a key population Facebook page in Vietnam revealed that 75% had never been in contact with a peer or outreach worker, 38% self-assessed as being at substantial risk of HIV infection, and 35% were motivated to test for HIV due to online content. Among 644 PrEP clients enrolled at a clinic in Ho Chi Minh City, 43% reported that online content motivated them to seek PrEP. These findings highlight the effectiveness of an online-to-offline (O2O) approach in reaching populations not connected to traditional outreach efforts, building trust, and successfully linking individuals to HIV testing, ART, and PrEP. The LINKAGES project in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), funded by USAID and PEPFAR and led by FHI 360, adapted index testing for men who have sex with men and female sex workers using two approaches: Voluntary Partner Referral (VPR) and Risk Network Referral (RNR). VPR allows people living with HIV (PLHIV) to voluntarily identify spouses, partners, and children at risk for HIV and offers various referral options, including client-referral, contact-referral, provider-referral, and dual-referral modalities. RNR extends beyond VPR by enabling PLHIV to informally link broader social and risk-network members to HIV testing and services through online and coupon-based referrals, without requiring disclosure of the referral source. From October to December 2018, 191 index cases (66 men who have sex with men, 110 female sex workers, and 15 clients of female sex workers) were offered index testing, and 143 agreed to provide contacts. A total of 169 contacts were listed, and 99 were tested, with high positivity rates observed. Index testing has proven effective in improving case detection among female sex workers, men who have sex with men, and clients of female sex workers in the DRC.
